module.title: Unit 9: Sociology of Urbanisation & Demographic Shifts
module.objective: Mampu menganalisis dampak migrasi desa-kota dan penuaan populasi dengan klausa adverbial komparatif mendalam.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Cities, Migration, and Ageing
subModules.grammarFocus: Comparative adverbial clauses, contrast clauses, parallel structures, and nuanced comparisons
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Urban growth, migration, population ageing, and public services

content.summary: Read about how migration from rural areas changes cities, and how longer life expectancy and lower birth rates affect communities. You will identify causes and consequences, compare population trends, and practise sentence patterns that show how two changes are connected.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use comparative clauses such as “The faster a city grows, the greater the pressure on its services becomes.” Practise contrast with while and whereas, parallels with just as, so too, and careful comparisons with not so much ... as.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Learn terms for urbanisation, rural-to-urban migration, demographic change, ageing populations, birth rates, infrastructure, and public services.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim each paragraph to find its main point. Then scan for causes, effects, comparisons, and examples. Use linking words to see how the writer connects different trends.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas in a B2 text about rural-to-urban migration and population ageing.
Locate details about why people move, which services face pressure, and how demographic patterns differ.
Recognize comparative adverbial clauses that describe linked changes.
Use contrast and parallel structures to compare social trends accurately.

contextWarmup.prompt: A town is growing quickly as young adults move there for work. Which change is most likely to place extra pressure on local services?
options: More residents needing transport, housing, and health services
Fewer people using the town's public facilities
A sudden fall in demand for homes and buses
contextWarmup.explanation: When the number of residents rises quickly, demand for housing and public services often increases too. If services do not expand at a similar rate, they may come under pressure.

rules: Use “The + comparative, the + comparative” to show that two changes are connected: “The faster the population grows, the harder it is to provide enough housing.”
Use while or whereas to contrast two situations: “Whereas city populations are growing, some rural areas are losing residents.”
Use “Just as ..., so too ...” to show that two events follow a similar pattern.
Use “not so much ... as ...” to correct or refine an explanation: “The problem is not so much a lack of space as an unequal distribution of housing.”

commonTrap.explanation: In comparative clauses, learners sometimes leave out the definite article or use an ordinary comparison instead of the paired structure. Look for two comparative parts that describe linked changes.
commonTrap.wrong: More quickly cities grow, greater the pressure becomes.
commonTrap.correct: The more quickly cities grow, the greater the pressure becomes.

content.contractionsTitle: Natural Spoken Contractions: Discussing Social Trends
content.contractionsSubtitle: Contractions are common in conversation, while formal reports usually use full forms:

contractions.subject: It
contractions.exampleFull: It is difficult to provide services when a city grows quickly.
contractions.exampleContracted: It's difficult to provide services when a city grows quickly.

contractions.subject: They
contractions.exampleFull: They are moving to the city for work.
contractions.exampleContracted: They're moving to the city for work.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Comparative and Contrast Clauses
grammarFormulas.description: Use these sentence blocks to make comparisons, describe linked trends, and contrast population patterns:

complements.text: the more quickly, the greater the pressure on services
just as employment attracts young adults, so too does access to education

items.meaning: urbanisasi; proses perpindahan penduduk ke kota
items.exampleSentence: Rapid urbanisation has changed the size and shape of many cities.
The demographic shift towards an older population affects public spending.

items.meaning: migrasi desa-kota; perpindahan penduduk dari pedesaan ke perkotaan
items.exampleSentence: Rural-to-urban migration is often linked to the search for education and work.

items.meaning: populasi menua; penduduk yang semakin tua rata-rata usianya

Growing communities need reliable public services, including transport and health care.
High population density can make housing and transport planning more difficult.
Improved health care has helped increase life expectancy in many countries.

content.passageTitle: Two Population Changes, One Planning Challenge
paragraphs: Across many regions, urbanisation is changing where people live and work. Rural-to-urban migration is often driven by jobs, education, and access to services, although not everyone who moves finds stable work or affordable housing. The faster a city grows, the greater the pressure on transport, water, and housing can become. This pressure is not so much a result of population size alone as of whether planning and investment keep pace.

At the same time, many countries are experiencing a demographic shift towards an ageing population. Lower birth rates and longer life expectancy mean that a larger share of residents may need health care and support in later life. Whereas some rural districts lose young adults, cities may attract them for study and employment. Just as cities need to plan for newcomers, so too must communities prepare for older residents. These trends differ, but both require reliable services and decisions based on local needs.

drills.instruction: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.meaning: The growth of towns and cities as more people live in them.
The number of births in a population during a period.
Pressure on facilities and systems when they cannot meet demand.
The average number of years a person is expected to live.

drills.instruction: Complete the sentence with the best term.
drills.sentence: When more people move from villages to cities, this is called ___.
options: rural-to-urban migration
life expectancy
birth rate

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How urban growth and population ageing create planning needs
Why rural communities should stop providing education
How every migrant finds affordable housing
questions.answer: How urban growth and population ageing create planning needs
questions.explanation: Both paragraphs describe population changes and explain why communities need to plan services in response.

questions.question: Which reasons for moving to cities are mentioned?
options: Jobs, education, and access to services
Lower life expectancy and fewer schools
A desire to reduce population density
questions.answer: Jobs, education, and access to services
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that migration is often driven by jobs, education, and access to services.

questions.question: According to the passage, what may happen as a city grows faster?
options: Pressure on transport, water, and housing may increase.
The need for planning and investment disappears.
All residents find stable work.
questions.answer: Pressure on transport, water, and housing may increase.
questions.explanation: The comparative clause states, “The faster a city grows, the greater the pressure” on these services can become.

questions.question: What does the phrase “not so much ... as ...” suggest about pressure on services?
options: Planning and investment matter, not population size alone.
Population size is the only cause of pressure.
Investment always causes population growth.
questions.answer: Planning and investment matter, not population size alone.
questions.explanation: The passage says the pressure is not so much a result of population size alone as of whether planning and investment keep pace.

questions.question: Which two trends contribute to an ageing population in the passage?
options: Lower birth rates and longer life expectancy
Higher birth rates and shorter life expectancy
More migration and higher population density
questions.answer: Lower birth rates and longer life expectancy
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly links lower birth rates and longer life expectancy with a larger share of older residents.

questions.question: What may a larger share of older residents need?
options: Health care and support in later life
More reasons to move to rural districts
Less access to public services
questions.answer: Health care and support in later life
questions.explanation: The passage explains that more residents may need health care and support as they grow older.

questions.question: What contrast does “Whereas” introduce?
options: Some rural districts lose young adults, while cities may attract them.
Cities lose all their residents as rural areas grow.
Older residents move only for employment.
questions.answer: Some rural districts lose young adults, while cities may attract them.
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts population changes in rural districts with the attraction of cities for study and employment.

questions.question: In “Just as cities need to plan for newcomers, so too must communities prepare for older residents,” what relationship is shown?
options: A parallel between two planning responsibilities
A cause-and-effect link between birth rates and migration
A difference between housing and transport
questions.answer: A parallel between two planning responsibilities
questions.explanation: The structure “Just as ..., so too ...” shows that planning for newcomers and preparing for older residents are parallel responsibilities.

questions.question: Does the passage say that everyone who moves to a city finds stable work or affordable housing?
options: No, it says that not everyone does.
Yes, it says all migrants find both.
It says that stable work is available only in rural areas.
questions.answer: No, it says that not everyone does.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explicitly notes that not everyone who moves finds stable work or affordable housing.

questions.question: What does the final sentence recommend for both population trends?
options: Reliable services and decisions based on local needs
The same service plan for every place
A focus on city residents rather than rural residents
questions.answer: Reliable services and decisions based on local needs
questions.explanation: The final sentence says that both trends require reliable services and decisions based on local needs.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Demographic Shifts and Urban Pressures

content.summary: This briefing prepares you to track comparative adverbial clauses and demographic terminology in rapid academic discussions. You will learn to detect fast spoken reductions and identify how speakers weigh contrasting global population patterns.
learningObjectives: Catch comparative structures used to explain demographic trends.
Identify specific causes and effects of rapid urban growth.
Notice how unstressed words and vowels link together in connected speech.

keyPhrases.note: A standard demographic term for population flow into metropolitan areas.
Used informally and academically to describe a sharp drop in statistics.

keyPhrases.meaning: beban atau tekanan pada sarana prasarana
keyPhrases.note: Refers to overcrowding and stress placed on transit, housing, and utilities.
A proportional comparative clause linking cause directly to effect.

connectedSpeech.note: The pronoun 'you' weakens to /jə/ in rapid conversational queries.
The suffix -ing reduces to an alveolar nasal /n/ before consonants.
The final alveolar stop /d/ links directly to the initial schwa /ə/.
The word 'than' loses its dental fricative and reduces to /ən/.

content.context: Alex and Morgan are sociology students sitting in a campus cafe, refining their presentation notes on global population shifts.
content.audioPrompt: Listen to the conversation between two friends.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Have you seen this migration data?
lines.translation: Apakah kamu sudah melihat data migrasi ini?

lines.speaker: Morgan
lines.text: Yes, cities keep growing so fast.
lines.translation: Ya, kota-kota terus tumbuh begitu cepat.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Villages lose their young workers quickly.
lines.translation: Desa-desa kehilangan pekerja muda mereka dengan cepat.

lines.speaker: Morgan
lines.text: Meanwhile, European cities are ageing rapidly.
lines.translation: Sementara itu, kota-kota di Eropa menua dengan cepat.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Birth rates plummeted across that region.
lines.translation: Angka kelahiran anjlok di seluruh wilayah itu.

lines.speaker: Morgan
lines.text: The bigger cities get, the harder planning is.
lines.translation: Semakin besar kota, semakin sulit perencanaannya.

lines.speaker: Alex

lines.speaker: Morgan
lines.text: Some countries invest heavily in infrastructure.
lines.translation: Beberapa negara berinvestasi besar-besaran pada infrastruktur.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Others struggle to handle the influx.

lines.translation: Kita sebaiknya berfokus pada perencanaan yang seimbang.

lines.text: Smart management matters more than restrictions.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Reading the Changing City

content.summary: Use comparative adverbial clauses to explain links between demographic trends, contrast rural and urban experiences, and draw parallels between periods of change. Support your claims with clear evidence and accurate punctuation.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Show a Proportional Relationship
blueprintItems.formula: The + comparative adjective/adverb + subject + verb, the + comparative adjective/adverb + subject + verb
blueprintItems.example: The more rapidly cities expand, the greater the strain on public infrastructure becomes.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Contrast Two Trends
blueprintItems.example: Whereas rural communities are experiencing population decline, major metropolitan areas continue to attract young professionals.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Draw a Parallel or Refine a Claim
blueprintItems.formula: Just as + clause 1, so (too) + clause 2; not so much + noun/gerund + as + noun/gerund
blueprintItems.example: Just as industrial growth drew workers to factory towns, so too has the digital economy attracted people to technology hubs.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma between the two clauses when a the-more-the-more construction begins with the first clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The faster a city grows the greater its demand for housing becomes.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The faster a city grows, the greater its demand for housing becomes.
mechanicsRules.why: The first clause introduces the relationship, and the comma separates it from the result.

mechanicsRules.rule: When a While or Whereas clause comes first, place a comma between it and the main clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: While younger adults move to cities older residents may remain in rural areas.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: While younger adults move to cities, older residents may remain in rural areas.
mechanicsRules.why: The comma marks the boundary between the opening contrast and the main statement.

mechanicsRules.rule: Keep parallel forms after not so much and as, and use a comma after an opening Just as clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The challenge is not so much finding workers as to train them.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The challenge is not so much finding workers as training them.
mechanicsRules.why: Both parts compare gerunds, and the comma separates the opening clause from the main clause.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Compare Rural and Urban Change
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a paragraph of 60 to 80 words comparing one demographic trend in a rural area with one in a city. Use While or Whereas to show contrast and include a the-more-the-more sentence to explain a relationship. Support your claims with a plausible example.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Whereas some rural districts are losing young adults, the nearby city is attracting workers in technology and healthcare. The more jobs the city offers, the more people may move there for work. This movement can increase demand for housing and public transport. However, the rural population may include a higher proportion of older residents, which can create a greater need for local care services.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Explain an Ageing Population
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short response of 50 to 70 words about one challenge linked to an ageing population. Use not so much ... as ... to make a precise distinction, and use Just as ... so too ... to draw a relevant parallel.
guidedLabChallenges.example: The challenge is not so much an ageing population as the shortage of accessible housing and care workers. Just as cities need to adapt transport for residents with limited mobility, so too do smaller towns need reliable health services. Local planning should take account of where older residents live and how easily they can reach essential support.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the the-more-the-more structure:
practicumQuestions.promptText: When cities expand more rapidly, they place greater pressure on public transport.
targetAnswers: The more rapidly cities expand, the greater the pressure they place on public transport.
The more rapidly cities grow, the greater the pressure they place on public transport.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a comparative phrase in each clause and put a comma between the first clause and the result.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with a suitable contrast conjunction:
practicumQuestions.promptText: __________ rural districts are losing young residents, major cities continue to attract new workers.
targetAnswers: While rural districts are losing young residents, major cities continue to attract new workers.
Whereas rural districts are losing young residents, major cities continue to attract new workers.
practicumQuestions.explanation: While and Whereas introduce a contrast between two trends. Place a comma after the opening clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas using Just as ... so too ...:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Improved transport can attract residents to cities. Reliable digital services can attract residents to smaller towns.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use Just as before the first clause and so too before the second.
targetAnswers: Just as improved transport can attract residents to cities, so too can reliable digital services attract residents to smaller towns.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This formal structure presents the two developments as parallel examples. The opening Just as clause is followed by a comma.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using not so much ... as ...:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The main concern is limited access to care rather than the ageing population itself.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the pattern not so much + noun phrase + as + noun phrase.
targetAnswers: The main concern is not so much the ageing population as limited access to care.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Not so much ... as ... shows that the second idea is a more accurate description of the concern.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalisation and punctuation:
practicumQuestions.promptText: the more people move to the city the higher housing demand becomes
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalise the first word and add a comma between the clauses.
targetAnswers: The more people move to the city, the higher housing demand becomes.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Start the sentence with a capital letter, separate the clauses with a comma, and end the sentence with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and capitalisation:
practicumQuestions.promptText: while rural areas may lose services older residents still need local support
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalise the opening word and add a comma after the introductory clause.
targetAnswers: While rural areas may lose services, older residents still need local support.
practicumQuestions.explanation: An opening While clause is followed by a comma before the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: __________ past industrial growth drew workers to factory towns, so too has the digital economy attracted people to technology hubs.
practicumQuestions.hint: Choose the phrase that introduces a formal parallel.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Just as ... so too ... draws a parallel between two developments.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the ideas using a the-more-the-more structure:
practicumQuestions.promptText: People live longer. The need for accessible housing increases.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the comparative form of long and begin: The longer ...
targetAnswers: The longer people live, the greater the need for accessible housing becomes.
The longer people live, the more the need for accessible housing increases.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The structure links two changes that increase together. Use a comma to separate the clauses.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write one sentence contrasting a trend in rural areas with a trend in cities. Use Whereas.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Include one plausible population or migration trend in each place.
practicumQuestions.hint: Begin with Whereas and place a comma before the main clause.
targetAnswers: Whereas rural areas are losing young adults, cities are attracting more workers.
Whereas smaller towns have ageing populations, cities continue to attract younger residents.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A suitable response presents two contrasting trends, uses Whereas to introduce the first clause, and separates the clauses with a comma.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write one sentence using not so much ... as ... to identify a challenge linked to an ageing population.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Your sentence should distinguish between population ageing and a related social or practical issue.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use parallel noun phrases after not so much and as.
targetAnswers: The challenge is not so much an ageing population as a lack of suitable care services.
The concern is not so much population ageing as the shortage of accessible housing.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This construction clarifies which issue is the more precise concern. Keep the two compared phrases grammatically parallel.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Cities, Migration and Ageing

content.summary: Practise discussing rural-to-urban migration, urbanisation and an ageing population. Explain causes and effects, compare changes over time, and support your views with clear examples. Use comparative adverbial clauses to show how one change happens in relation to another.
content.audioGuidance: Speak at a steady pace and group ideas into short thought units. Stress key content words, especially terms such as urbanisation and infrastructure strain. In comparative clauses, make the relationship clear: As more people move to cities, pressure on public transport increases. Use a falling tone to finish a statement and a rising tone when checking or asking a genuine question.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.explanation: Keep vowel sounds distinct in words such as shift, birth and ageing. Avoid shortening the vowel in ageing so much that it sounds like a different word.

pillars.name: Word Stress
pillars.target: Correct stress in longer topic words
pillars.explanation: Give the main stress to the correct syllable: ur-ban-i-SA-tion, de-mo-GRA-phic and in-fra-STRUC-ture. Clear stress helps listeners recognise unfamiliar academic vocabulary.

pillars.name: Comparative Clauses
pillars.explanation: Use structures such as the more..., the greater... and as..., so... to compare trends. Pause briefly between the two parts when needed, but keep them connected.

pillars.name: Sentence Intonation
pillars.explanation: Let your voice fall at the end of a complete explanation. Use a rising tone for a yes-or-no question or when inviting confirmation, rather than raising your voice at the end of every sentence.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress falls on the fourth syllable in urbanisation, but on the final syllable in urbanise.
The main stress shifts from the third syllable in demographic to the second in demography.
The main stress shifts from the second syllable in migration to the first in migrant.
The main stress stays on STRUC when the word changes from infrastructure to infrastructural.

drills.targetText: As more people move to cities, pressure on public transport increases.
drills.phonetic: /əz mɔː ˈpiːpəl muːv tə ˈsɪtiz, ˈpreʃə ɒn ˈpʌblɪk ˈtrænspɔːt ɪnˈkriːsɪz/
drills.focus: Comparative adverbial clause and sentence rhythm
drills.hint: Link the opening clause smoothly, then stress pressure and increases.

drills.targetText: The more rapidly a city grows, the greater the infrastructure strain becomes.
drills.phonetic: /ðə mɔː ˈræpɪdli ə ˈsɪti ɡrəʊz, ðə ˈɡreɪtə ði ˈɪnfrəˌstrʌktʃə streɪn bɪˈkʌmz/
drills.hint: Keep the two halves balanced and emphasise rapidly, greater and strain.

drills.targetText: An ageing population can increase demand for health and care services.
drills.phonetic: /ən ˈeɪdʒɪŋ ˌpɒpjəˈleɪʃən kən ɪnˈkriːs dɪˈmɑːnd fə helθ ən keə ˈsɜːvɪsɪz/
drills.hint: Stress ageing, population and demand, while keeping can short and unstressed.

drills.targetText: How might a lower birth rate affect the size of the workforce?
drills.phonetic: /haʊ maɪt ə ˈləʊə bɜːθ reɪt əˈfekt ðə saɪz əv ðə ˈwɜːkfɔːs/
drills.focus: Rising question intonation and key vocabulary
drills.hint: Use a rising tone at the end of the question and stress birth rate and workforce.

roleplay.context: You are discussing population changes at a community planning meeting. One participant is concerned about fast urban growth, while the other is presenting evidence about migration and ageing.

turns.speaker: Community Planner
turns.text: More families are moving here from nearby villages. What changes have you noticed in the city?
turns.translation: Semakin banyak keluarga pindah ke sini dari desa-desa sekitar. Perubahan apa yang kamu lihat di kota ini?

turns.speaker: Sociology Student
turns.text: As the population grows, demand for housing and public transport rises. The more quickly the city expands, the harder it is to keep services affordable.
turns.translation: Seiring bertambahnya jumlah penduduk, kebutuhan akan perumahan dan transportasi umum meningkat. Semakin cepat kota berkembang, semakin sulit menjaga layanan tetap terjangkau.

turns.speaker: Community Planner
turns.text: That is a concern. How could an ageing population affect the services we need?
turns.translation: Itu menjadi perhatian. Bagaimana populasi yang menua dapat memengaruhi layanan yang kita butuhkan?

turns.speaker: Sociology Student
turns.text: As the share of older residents increases, the need for accessible transport and eldercare grows. We should plan for both new arrivals and long-term residents.
turns.translation: Seiring meningkatnya proporsi penduduk lanjut usia, kebutuhan akan transportasi yang mudah diakses dan perawatan lansia juga bertambah. Kita perlu merencanakan kebutuhan pendatang baru dan penduduk lama.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds about a place that has changed as people have moved there.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a town or city you know that has grown or changed because of migration.
storyPoints: Describe what the place was like before and what it is like now
Explain why people moved there and what opportunities they were seeking
Compare how services or daily life changed as the population grew
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: As more people moved into the city, demand for housing grew faster than local services could expand.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /əz mɔː ˈpiːpəl muːvd ˈɪntə ðə ˈsɪti, dɪˈmɑːnd fə ˈhaʊzɪŋ ɡruː ˈfɑːstə ðən ˈləʊkəl ˈsɜːvɪsɪz kəd ɪkˈspænd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Tell a connected story and use a comparative adverbial clause to explain how growth and change were related.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 30 seconds about how an ageing population may affect a community.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell a short story about a community adjusting to a growing number of older residents.
storyPoints: Describe a change in the community's age profile
Explain how the need for transport, healthcare or care services changed
Suggest how planning ahead could improve life for older and younger residents
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The larger the older population becomes, the more important accessible transport and local care services are.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈlɑːdʒə ði ˈəʊldə ˌpɒpjəˈleɪʃən bɪˈkʌmz, ðə mɔː ɪmˈpɔːtənt əkˈsesəbəl ˈtrænspɔːt ən ˈləʊkəl keə ˈsɜːvɪsɪz ɑː/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Organise your account around a clear change and its consequences. Use the larger..., the more... structure accurately.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live roleplay. Respond to the planner, explain one pressure caused by population growth, and propose a practical response.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: The city planner wants to know how rapid urbanisation is affecting local services.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: At a city planning meeting, discuss the effects of rural-to-urban migration on housing, transport and sanitation. Use a comparative clause to connect the speed of growth with the level of pressure.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a sociology student who has studied local population trends. Give one example and suggest a realistic action.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The faster the city grows, the greater the pressure on housing and public transport.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈfɑːstə ðə ˈsɪti ɡrəʊz, ðə ˈɡreɪtə ðə ˈpreʃə ɒn ˈhaʊzɪŋ ən ˈpʌblɪk ˈtrænspɔːt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Answer the planner directly, support your point with an example and offer a practical response.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live roleplay. Explain why people are leaving rural areas and how the change affects both places.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A local journalist is interviewing you about rural-to-urban migration.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A journalist is preparing a report on why rural residents move to a nearby city and what this means for rural communities and urban services.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a community researcher. Give balanced comments about jobs, education and the services available in each place.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: As job opportunities in the city increase, more young adults may decide to leave rural areas.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /əz dʒɒb ˌɒpəˈtjuːnətiz ɪn ðə ˈsɪti ɪnˈkriːs, mɔː jʌŋ ˈædʌlts meɪ dɪˈsaɪd tə liːv ˈrʊərəl ˈeəriəz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Compare the opportunities and challenges in rural and urban areas without presenting migration as entirely positive or negative.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live roleplay. Discuss the effect of an ageing population and recommend a service improvement.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A council officer asks what the area should do as its population gets older.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A council is reviewing local services because the average age of residents is rising. Discuss accessible transport, healthcare or community care.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a resident representative. Explain which need is becoming more urgent and why.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The more residents need support at home, the greater the need for well-trained care workers.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə mɔː ˈrezɪdənts niːd səˈpɔːt ət həʊm, ðə ˈɡreɪtə ðə niːd fə ˌwel ˈtreɪnd keə ˈwɜːkəz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Explain how a demographic change affects a specific service and make a clear recommendation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Take part in a live roleplay. Respond to a policy adviser and compare two possible approaches to demographic change.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A policy adviser asks whether the city should focus on attracting workers or supporting older residents.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: In a policy discussion, consider how a city can respond to a low birth rate and an ageing population while also meeting the needs of new arrivals.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are an adviser who wants a balanced policy. Compare support for families, workers and older residents.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The more effectively a city supports families and older residents, the better it can respond to long-term demographic change.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə mɔː ɪˈfektɪvli ə ˈsɪti səˈpɔːts ˈfæməliz ən ˈəʊldə ˈrezɪdənts, ðə ˈbetə ɪt kən rɪˈspɒnd tə ˌlɒŋ ˈtɜːm ˌdeməˈɡræfɪk tʃeɪndʒ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Compare the policy options and explain why a balanced response may be more effective.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for 20 to 30 seconds. Use urbanisation, infrastructure strain and rural-to-urban migration accurately in a short explanation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Explain how rural-to-urban migration can contribute to infrastructure strain during rapid urbanisation.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: When rural-to-urban migration speeds up, rapid urbanisation can put infrastructure under strain.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wen ˌrʊərəl tə ˈɜːbən maɪˈɡreɪʃən spiːdz ʌp, ˈræpɪd ˌɜːbənaɪˈzeɪʃən kən pʊt ˈɪnfrəˌstrʌktʃə ˈʌndə streɪn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use each term in a meaningful sentence and make the cause-and-effect link clear.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the idea aloud using a comparative adverbial clause with the more..., the more... pattern.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Begin with: The more quickly a city grows... Then explain one effect on housing or public services.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The more quickly a city grows, the more difficult it becomes to provide affordable housing.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə mɔː ˈkwɪkli ə ˈsɪti ɡrəʊz, ðə mɔː ˈdɪfɪkəlt ɪt bɪˈkʌmz tə prəˈvaɪd əˈfɔːdəbəl ˈhaʊzɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Keep the comparative structure parallel and use a clear consequence in the second clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the target sentence three times. Keep the main stress on the third syllable of demographic.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Practise the word demographic in a sentence about population change.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: A demographic shift can change a city's need for housing and care.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ə ˌdeməˈɡræfɪk ʃɪft kən tʃeɪndʒ ə ˈsɪtiz niːd fə ˈhaʊzɪŋ ən keə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Stress the GRA syllable in demographic and speak the whole sentence without adding extra stress to every word.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the statement with falling intonation, then ask a follow-up yes-or-no question with rising intonation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: First say, The birth rate has fallen. Then ask, Could that affect the workforce?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The birth rate has fallen. Could that affect the workforce?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈbɜːθ reɪt hæz ˈfɔːlən. kəd ðæt əˈfekt ðə ˈwɜːkfɔːs/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Let your voice fall at the end of the statement and rise at the end of the yes-or-no question.
